name: Western Pantar
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Word stress is transcribed here only where relevant to the correspondence in question (e.g., ‘dog1’). In most of the modern languages stress is on the penultimate syllable; however, stress may also be attracted to heavy syllables, as in Teiwa jiˈvar ‘dog’. In addition, stress may be phonemically contrastive in some languages, as in Western Pantar baˈwa ‘conch shell’ vs. ˈbawa ‘drum’. [p. 55] || Western Pantar geminate stops occur predictably before stressed final vowels (even if the syllable in question is no longer closed in modern Western Pantar). [Schapper et al., p. 121]
new_statements.citation: Holton, Gary & Laura C. Robinson. 2017. The internal history of the Alor-Pantar language family. In Marian Klamer (ed.), The Alor-Pantar languages: History and typology, 2nd ed. (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 3), 49-89. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.437098
new_statements.locator: p. 55 (PDF page 69), transcription paragraph at the head of the sound-correspondence section; supplementary sentence: Schapper, Huber & van Engelenhoven 2017, same volume, p. 121 (PDF page 135)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only open statement is a comparative-paper remark by the language's describer: across modern Alor-Pantar languages stress is generally penultimate (with attraction to heavy syllables), but in Western Pantar stress is (at least partly) phonemically contrastive, as in baˈwa 'conch shell' vs. ˈbawa 'drum'; Schapper et al. add that WP geminates occur predictably before stressed final vowels, i.e. final-stressed words exist alongside penultimate-stressed ones and stress position is not fully predictable from the segmental string. A penultimate default with lexically specified final stress (historically from closed final syllables) is the most likely picture, but no WP-specific rule is stated in any source opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress attraction to heavy syllables noted for the family (Teiwa example); contrastive pairs in WP; gemination linked to (historically closed) stressed final syllables; Heston (2016: 288, as cited) says the stress-based gemination account does not hold for geminate s and l.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms in comparative wordlists; the remark is a transcription note in a historical-comparative chapter, not a phonology section of a WP grammar. Holton's WP data are mostly the Tubbe dialect (Holton 2010: 98).
new_statements.identity_note: Western Pantar = Lamma (also Tubbe, Mauta, Pantar Barat), glottocode lamm1241, ISO lev. Holton's data are mainly the Tubbe dialect (Holton 2010: 98); Stokhof 1975 lists the same language as 'Lamma' with dialects Kalondama, Mauta/Tubal (= Tubbe) and Biangwala. Nitbani et al. 2001 call it Bahasa Lamma. No separate glottocodes for the dialects.
